the rate of increase of CSR assurance is high, the rate of increase is higher for non-audit assurance providers than for audit firms, and the assurance standards used are mostly not aligned to King III requirements.
the rate of CSR assurance by auditor is not as high as that by non-auditors.
the audit profession is still the most prominent provider of CSR assurance, but that non-auditor CSR assurance providers are gaining ground.

the assurance of CSR disclosures and not the assurance of sustainability disclosures, which is a separate and more complex issue.
the implications for CSR assurance by the auditing profession.
the assurance providers, the assurance standards used, the assurance report contents and assurance opinions provided, and the implications of these findings for the assurance profession.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the audit profession is still the most important assurance provider, but that non-auditor providers are gaining market share.
the auditing profession is still the most popular assurance provider, but that the growth of the non-audit profession is significant and may continue to be significant.
the audit profession has not been able to take a leadership role in CSR assurance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no one-size-fits all assurance model.
the audit profession is losing market share to the non-audit assurance providers.
the audit profession is not the only provider of CSR assurance and that non-auditors are increasingly providing assurance on CSR.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CSR assurance has grown substantially in South Africa and that the audit profession has not been able to capitalise on this growth.
the assurance market is becoming more competitive and that companies are becoming more selective in their choice of assurance providers.
the audit profession is not the only assurance provider for CSR and that companies are using non-auditor providers for CSR assurance.
